article.plain_text:
three days ago Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2, and the internet has not stopped shipping since.
an Anthropic engineer typed one casual sentence and got a full shooter game with its own 3D models, sounds and textures. 8 hours, zero help from him. a guy who never wrote code built an open-world RPG with a map twice the size of Skyrim in 4 days. someone asked for a GTA-style city and was driving through it 2 hours 14 minutes later.
meanwhile most people still use the strongest model on earth to rewrite emails.
 
that gap is the whole story. a year ago the best AI could fully finish 2.5% of real freelance projects. Fable 5.2 finishes 41.3%. sites, apps, 3D, data, design: the work people pay agencies thousands for.
the people who learn to point it at a thing this month will own the next year. one person and one model now build what used to need a studio.
and you do not need to code. by sunday you can have your own game, website or app running from one prompt.
this is the full course. one system, eight things you can build with it this weekend, and the exact prompts.
and there is a clock on it. until November 16, Fable 5.2 is included in the $20 Pro plan. after that it runs on paid credits.
01. why Fable 5.2 changes what one person can build
02. the setup: where to click
03. the system in one minute
04. eight things to build: game, film, device, app, website, business, music, team
05. your first weekend
06. four lines that make every build finish
07. the whole course on one screen
before we start, follow me on X and join my Telegram channel where i post more AI content every day. both are free.
X: https://x.com/Argona0x
Telegram: https://t.me/+r0clI4-MMC03ZjAy
 
01. why Fable 5.2 changes what one person can build
Fable 5.2 is the top model from Anthropic, the company behind Claude. you give it a goal, it works on it for hours by itself, checks its own work and comes back with a finished thing.
older models handed you a piece of code and stopped. Fable plans the whole project, writes it, runs it, looks at the result and fixes what is broken.
you can see the jump in three numbers:
it finishes real jobs: on a test made of real paid freelance projects it completes 41.3%. Opus 5.5, the everyday Claude model, completes 21.3%. the previous Fable completed 17.9%.
hardware works too: from a one-paragraph prompt it designed three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, cases and software. all three worked without a single fix to the circuit.
days-long runs: one Anthropic engineer gave it an empty folder. it ran over 1,000 AI workers for 8 days and came back with a working operating system that boots on a laptop.
the inside proof: over 90% of the code merged into Anthropic's own codebase is now written by Claude.
 
the hard part is no longer the building. the hard part is knowing what to ask for.
the skill that pays now is describing the finished thing
 
02. the setup: where to click
you need a paid Claude plan. Free does not include Fable.
open the Claude app: web, desktop or phone.
open the model picker and choose Fable 5.2. it is never selected by default, so check it every new chat.
small builds (a game in one file, a toy, a page): stay in the chat. Claude shows the result as an artifact, a working page next to the chat that you can open and share by link.
big builds (a film, a device, a full app): open Claude Desktop and switch to the Code tab. same model, but it works with real files on your computer. type `/effort` and pick high.
pro move: use Opus 5.5 for small edits and spend Fable on the one big job. Anthropic recommends exactly this, and it keeps your limits for the builds that matter.
 
you will see the first result in minutes. big builds run for hours while you do something else.
 
03. the system in one minute
the classic first prompt is "build me a universe". one huge wish with no edges. it burns a whole week of limits and comes back as a pretty demo.
the people getting magic give Fable four things every time:
the thing: what it is, who it is for, how small. "a tiny level", "one HTML file", "one page".
the reference: a picture, a link, a drawing, a song you love.
the self-check: "after each part, run it yourself, screenshot it and fix what looks wrong."
the finish line: "don't stop until a stranger could use it for 10 minutes without a bug."
one more line comes straight from Anthropic's own guide. tell Fable the project is its own, and it cleans up and restructures its work in about 75% of runs instead of under 10%.
 
 
every module below uses this exact shape. or paste this whole article into Claude and say: build module 03 for me.
a self-check and a finish line turn a demo into a product
 
04. eight things to build
each module has the same form: what you get, who already did it, three steps, the prompt, and what "done" looks like.
01. a game
the fastest way to see what Fable can do is to ask it for a game.
games were the biggest thing people built in the first three days. at least 25 different people posted one. Fable writes the code, the 3D models, the textures and even the sounds, then plays its own game to find bugs.
Felix Rieseberg from Anthropic sent one casual sentence and got Saltline, a shooter where every model and texture is written in code. 8 hours, no feedback from him, 4.2M views on the post. Lex Toumbourou gave it his nephew's drawings and woke up to a 12-level beat 'em up with 18 playable heroes, the family dog included.
 
pick a game you loved as a kid.
write its loop in one line: what you do, what you get, what you spend it on.
paste the prompt and leave it for an hour.
@ericmaskfr sent this prompt for his 80s Miami crime city and was playing it 2 hours 14 minutes later:
 
done means: a friend plays 10 minutes on their phone without asking you how.
02. a film
Fable 5.2 can direct a whole 3D film, and nobody has to touch a camera.
it does not draw the video. it writes code that builds a 3D scene in Blender (a free 3D program), places the cameras and lights, animates everything and renders the frames.
Riley Brown did it live on stream with one prompt: a room with a desk and a laptop, 13 camera shots, golden hour into night into sunrise, music and sound effects. Fable rented 10 GPUs, rendered it in 4K in 52 minutes, and the whole film cost $5.75. 847k views. @xikhar got a Bugatti Tourbillon modeled part by part, interior included, in 2.5 hours from one prompt and a few photos.
 
install Blender, it is free.
in the Code tab, ask Claude to set up Blender MCP, a free plugin that lets Claude drive Blender for you.
paste the prompt with one reference image.
 
done means: a 20-second clip you would post today.
03. a device
Fable 5.2 designs real hardware: the circuit board, the case and the code.
it draws the board in KiCad (free board design software), picks the parts, designs the case and writes the software. you upload the files to an online factory, and the board and the printed case arrive by mail. no lab, no 3D printer needed.
Anthropic gave it one paragraph per device and got three: a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone and a handheld virtual pet. the boards were ready for manufacturing in under a day. all three worked without a single fix to the circuit. the whole speakerphone brief was one line: "a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna."
 
write what the device does in one sentence, like Anthropic did.
install KiCad, it is free.
paste the prompt in the Code tab on high effort.
 
done means: both checks show 0 errors and the parts list fits on one screen.
04. an app
if you ever thought "someone should build an app for this", that someone is now you.
apps are where Fable pays off every day. one file, saved on your computer, built around exactly how you work.
a Reddit user built a webcam X-ray mirror: skull, brain and muscles pinned to your face, hand bones that follow your fingers. first working version in under an hour, in one chat, 4.1k upvotes. a neurologist in the comments asked to use it with patients. Claire Vo built a cozy typewriter app with timers, notecards and a dot-matrix print button, and is thinking of shipping it for real.
 
write down one thing you do every day that annoys you.
describe the screen you wish existed.
paste the prompt in the chat and open the artifact.
 
done means: you open it every morning for three days straight.
05. a website
a site that looks like an agency built it, without paying the agency.
the secret is rules you can measure. "make it modern" gets you a template. screen sizes, spacing and contrast get you a site that looks expensive. a thread with exactly these rules got 3,600 bookmarks in two days.
@0xMovez built an interactive robotics school with Fable: 8 real boards in 3D, you place the chips, solder them and wire real circuits. every 3D model was generated in code, no ready-made files. 333k views.
 
collect 2 sites you love and your own text.
paste the prompt with both links.
open it on your phone before anything else.
 
done means: you send the link to someone and they ask who designed it.
06. a business
Fable 5.2 can find a business, check that people want it and build the first version.
Ethan Mollick, a Wharton professor, gave it one line: "launch a business to make me money, I want at least $20,000 in a year. it should take no more than 20 minutes a month from me, you do all the rest." Fable screened 22 ideas and picked Prebid Brief, a lead service for park and water projects. then it read meeting agendas from 201 city and county governments to fill it with real leads.
Jump Trading's head of AI research said Fable is "incredible at playing every major role within a research system".
 
write what you are good at and how many hours a week you have.
paste the prompt and let it research for an hour.
read the one-page plan and approve the next step.
 
done means: one page with the idea, 10 real buyers with links, and a demo you can show them.
07. music
it writes the song, builds the instrument and builds the studio.
Fable makes sound with code: no samples, no plugins. it can build you an instrument in the browser, then play it.
Kieran Klaassen, a former film composer, built his dream ambient music app in a week of evenings: synths, effects, hardware controller support and an AI inside the app he asks for "birds in Lydian". @The_Alex built a music app where you ask for a track and it opens the project and writes it, 112k views. @peach2k2 got a full love song in one prompt, 388k views.
 
pick one song you love and write its mood in three words.
paste the prompt in the chat.
press play, then ask for the changes you hear.
 
done means: a 30-second loop you made, exported and playing on your phone.
08. a team
the final level: Fable 5.2 runs a team of cheaper AI workers and only calls you for decisions.
Fable is the expensive brain. Opus 5.5 workers do the typing for half the price. Fable plans the job, hands out tasks, checks every result and gives out the next one.
this is how Anthropic built the operating system in 8 days with over 1,000 AI workers. a team of about 1,000 Fable workers also rewrote one of the most famous math proofs in history, Fermat's Last Theorem, so a computer could check every line. it took 30 hours. the same team on Opus 5.5 got 26% of the way in 18 hours. the "conductor" setup @lennox_saint posted got 12,000 bookmarks.
 
open the Code tab and pick Fable 5.2.
give it one big goal: a full app, a whole game, a business launch.
paste the conductor prompt under the goal.
this is the prompt from @lennox_saint, word for word:
 
done means: you come back to a finished project and a short recap of who did what.
 
05. your first weekend
one build per weekend is enough to be ahead of almost everyone you know.
friday evening, 10 minutes: pick one module. collect the reference: a picture, a link, a song.
saturday morning: send the prompt on high effort. go live your life.
saturday evening: open it on your phone and your laptop. write the 3 things you would change and send them in one message.
sunday: record a 30-second screen video of it working and post it.
that video is the part most people skip. it is also the part that gets you clients, followers and the next idea.
 
one finished build beats a hundred saved prompts
 
06. four lines that make every build finish
these four lines are why some people get a finished product and others get a half-built demo.
tell it to finish: at medium effort Fable sometimes stops and lists what is left. add: "do not stop while you still owe work I asked for. carry on with everything that does not need my answer."
make it prove it: "do not report a check as passed unless you ran it." add screenshots or a test, and Fable shows you evidence instead of a promise.
name what not to touch: "don't touch the desktop layout." "don't change the field order." one line keeps a small fix small.
edit instead of arguing: when an answer is wrong, click edit on your last message, fix the prompt and send it again. arguing in the chat burns limits.
 
and keep the split from chapter 02. Opus 5.5 for small edits, Fable 5.2 for the big build.
the builders shipping every weekend all use the same four lines
 
07. the whole course on one screen
 
 
pick one row tonight. send the prompt before you go to sleep.
by sunday you will have built something most people still think takes a studio, a team and a year.
and remember the clock. Fable 5.2 is included in Pro until November 16.
if you want to stay up to date with everything happening in AI, follow me on X and Telegram:
X: https://x.com/Argona0x
Telegram: https://t.me/+r0clI4-MMC03ZjAy

article.plain_text:
Claude, GPT and Grok are three families of models, one per company, and each wins different jobs. almost nobody sends each job to its winner, lets another family check it, or prices it by the finished result.
you use AI every day for code, sites, research or marketing, and every job goes to one model. so what that model is weak at comes back weak.
this guide puts one AI employee on Claude, GPT and Grok and sends each job to the model that wins it. an AI employee is an AI in your Slack or Teams that does the jobs you send it.
public tests put Claude Opus 5.5, in Anthropic's own coding app, first as a coding agent, an AI that edits your project's files by itself, and first for web apps. GPT-6.1 Sol gives the most answers with a real source, and only Grok 4.7 searches X live (links in 01).
since 12 october, Grok comes with a paid X plan, so all three cost:
$48 a month at the cheapest plans, $600 at the top ones.
the three can sit in one place: viktor, an AI employee. he runs on all three, you set which one takes each job, and he waits for your yes on anything that matters.
tonight, list the last ten jobs you gave AI. 01 sorts that list by model.
a top model is the strongest and priciest model in a family, like Claude Opus 5.5.
the route starts with one question and ends with one setup:
who is good at what
what one job costs
a second family checks
a top model where it counts
where the money goes, and scripts
my own test, 7 november. i asked viktor "where are my credits going?". credits are the one balance every job he runs spends from, on any family.
in under a minute he named the five chats that cost the most.
my plain messages, with no model asked, all ran on a top model.
1,074 of the 1,999 credits my test had spent. more than half.
viktor changed nothing until my yes. i approved one fix: a cheaper default for every chat.
 
 
before we start, follow me on X and join my Telegram channel where i post more AI content every day. both are free.
X: https://x.com/Argona0x
Telegram: https://t.me/+r0clI4-MMC03ZjAy
 
the fast route: one question, two answers
from here on, viktor leads each part, and each part also shows the way with one plan. this route gets all three families into one chat tonight.
with viktor: one question, two commands
viktor is an AI employee who lives in a Slack or Microsoft Teams workspace, your team's space in the app.
viktor runs all three families from one balance of credits, with no separate Claude, ChatGPT or X plan. in my test nothing else was connected.
Slack's free plan costs nothing, and a workspace you create makes you its owner.
in a work Slack or Teams, an admin installs him.
with no Slack yet, open slack.com/get-started, enter your email and press Continue. then enter the inbox code and press Create a workspace.
the sign-up link is in my first reply:
open that link and press Get Started for Free.
choose Continue with Slack or Continue with Microsoft Teams, and sign in.
finish the setup (Skip, I'll connect tools later is fine). his first message arrives in your chat.
if sign-up asks for a card, add it: a quick check with no charge that adds free starter credits.
use the code ARGONA100 from my first reply when you sign up.
after the starter credits, choose a plan from the same link.
a scheduled job is a task he runs on a timer, like a morning plan.
send viktor this first, so he knows your work and when to stop:
 
a command is a word with `!` at the start of a message. it changes that one reply only.
`!fast` asks for a quick answer, and `!deep` is for a hard problem.
an admin picks the model behind each one. in a new workspace, `!deep` is set to Use default model, and then it does nothing.
his web app is the site where you signed up. there, open Settings, the Model tab, and under Model overrides set `!deep` to Ultra, his team mode for the hardest work.
then ask one question from tonight's list, with `!fast`, then `!deep`.
on 7 november, each reply came back in about 40 seconds, ending on Fast reply or Deep reply.
 
without viktor: two chats
open two new chats in your paid app. in one, pick the family's quick model, its fast and cheap one: Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Terra.
Grok has one current model, Grok 4.7.
in the other, its top model. ask both the same question.
one question, two answers, and you see which jobs a quick answer covers.
jobs the quick answer covered stay on it. 01 sorts the rest by model.
 
01. who is good at what
before you pay for a second plan, learn which model wins each job you run. your code, pages and research come back better.
backend is the server side of an app, and terminal work means typing commands into a terminal, the text window developers run programs in.
an arena is a public site where people pick the better of two blind answers.
the job card puts each job next to where to start and the proof behind it:
 
 
each row links to its proof, in order: 
https://www.linkedin.com/posts/artificial-analysis_announcing-artificial-analysis-coding-agent-activity-7519196310160187392-sz2O · https://llmbenchmark.ai/best/web-development · https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5 · https://arxiv.org/html/2607.21656v1 · https://truestandard.ai/which-ai-hallucinates-the-least · https://x.ai/news/x-subscription · https://arena.ai/leaderboard/chat/text/creative-writing · https://arena.ai/leaderboard/image/text-to-image
on ChatGPT Plus, the chat runs GPT-6 Astra, the strongest model in OpenAI's line. Sol, the one the test scored, is not in that chat yet, so ask Astra for a source on every claim.
keep sourced research off quick models. TrueStandard, the source test behind the card, found Claude Haiku 5.5 made up almost one source in five.
paste this with your list of ten into the chat you already use:
 
back comes each job with a model next to it and a mark on the costly ones. the proof moves with every release, so run the sort again when a new model comes out.
with viktor: one model per job
the card pays off only when each job lands on the card's model, and viktor gives you two ways to route each one.
in his web app, click the model name in the message box, choose Custom model and pick from the list. it groups the models by company: Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI.
pick before the first message of a job. the picker warns that a switch mid-chat re-reads the whole chat and uses more credits.
in Slack, a message and its replies form a thread, and each thread is one chat with him.
Slack has no model picker in the message box, so each family gets its own command. in Settings, the Model tab, under Model overrides, type a name into the empty field that shows `!research`, press Add command and pick its model.
i added `!claude`, `!gpt` and `!grok`, and viktor answered each one. a message that starts with one of them runs on that model.
when i later asked viktor where my credits went, his table listed each chat with the model it ran on. that is how you check the routing yourself.
 
without viktor: one app per family
open the family's own app for each job, Claude, ChatGPT or Grok. start a new chat there and pick the card's model in its model menu.
every job on your list now has a model and the proof behind it.
the marks matter in 02, where they decide which jobs get a top model.
 
02. what all three cost, and what one job costs
you either pay three bills, or pay one and redo the jobs it is weak at.
with viktor: what each chat spent
viktor's Usage page shows what each chat and scheduled job spent, and which model did the work. only an admin sees it.
before my test, it said Claude's top model did 94% of my work in the last 30 days.
on test day, my `!fast` reply ran longer than my `!deep` reply and cost about a fifth more.
try both on your own question, and keep the cheaper answer that is good enough.
the price of a finished answer
a model that writes more, takes more steps or needs more tries spends more on the same job.
ChatGPT is the app for GPT, and Grok comes with a paid X plan. at list price, the three cost this much a month:
 
ChatGPT Pro comes at two levels, $100 and $200, so it sits in two rows. prices from claude.com/pricing, OpenAI's help center and x.ai, checked 5 november.
models bill by the token, a small piece of text. the coding agent index from 01 prices each task through the API, the pay-per-use door that developers call from code.
there, GPT-6.1 Sol, in OpenAI's coding app, cost $1.50 a task. Grok 4.7, in xAI's, cost $9.48 a task and scored lower.
 
on a monthly plan the bill stays fixed, so the plan's limit decides how far each model goes. SemiAnalysis, a chip and AI research firm, says to judge the plan, the model and the work together.
a practitioner write-up on ctxt.dev, on earlier models, found the top model solves hard problems on the first try more often. on routine jobs it is just more expensive with no upside.
so a job's price is the price of the finished answer, redos included. a cheap answer you redo three times costs three runs.
fill this cost sheet from your list of ten, with your best guess at the tries each job takes:
 
the rows with the most tries are the jobs that cost you the most.
price every job by the finished answer, and the cheapest model changes job by job.
the yes column is your costly list, and 04 keeps it on a top model.
 
03. let a second family check the first
a second model catches the bug or the wrong source before your users or your client do.
code: one family builds, the other checks
the family on your card builds the code, and the other family reviews it.
in one paper, on earlier models, Claude checking GPT's code raised the pass rate, the share of tasks done right, from 72% to 90%, and GPT checking Claude's code lowered it. https://arxiv.org/html/2607.21656v1
setups developers posted this autumn run the other order: Claude builds and GPT reviews. try both orders once on one feature, and keep the one that finds more real bugs. https://x.com/romainlanz/status/2111231027171491932 · https://x.com/Voxyz_ai/status/2116575932957762004 · https://x.com/curiouswavefn/status/2111665926156292297
with viktor: both families in one chat
start the job with the builder's command, `!claude` or `!gpt`. when the code is back, send the review in the same chat with the other family's command.
for your own work, first paste the code from your branch, the copy of the project where your new work lives. the review asks how to reproduce each bug, that is, how to make it happen again:
 
in my test, a `!gpt` message got back a short function that adds up expenses from a spreadsheet file. viktor's review came back in 43 seconds: a verdict, then each bug with its line, what breaks, a way to reproduce it and a fix.
viktor marked one point "not sure" instead of guessing, and the whole chat cost about as much as two `!fast` replies. only the bugs that reproduce go back to the model that wrote the code.
without viktor: the other family's app, or a brand-new chat
in the other family's app, paste your code and the same review without its command.
with one plan, finish the work first. then press New chat, keep the same model and paste the same review.
in a coding agent, close it and start it again. then the review has no memory of the build.
a write-up on stephens.page found that a brand-new chat caught real missed bugs in over half of the features it checked, about as well as a second family. https://stephens.page/blog/fresh-eyes-beat-a-second-family/paper/
sites: assets first, then code
a builder's tip: make the UI assets, the icons, pictures and backgrounds a page uses, first, with the model in the job card's images row, then have Opus 5.5 code the page. https://x.com/ann_nnng/status/2109463240527040796
send references or your design system along, the colors, fonts and spacing your brand uses.
open a new Claude chat on Opus 5.5, attach the images and paste this:
 
you get the code for a page built only from your images, and it stops to show you before adding anything new.
posts: Grok finds, Claude writes
Grok searches X live, and Opus 5.5 leads the creative-writing votes. so one post uses both, in one viktor chat:
 
in my test i asked for two posts. viktor's `!grok` answer took about two minutes and came back with two posts, their links and what the replies said.
then send the answer on:
 
the draft that comes back answers the strongest post, and nothing goes out. without viktor, send the first message to the Grok app and the second to a chat on Opus 5.5, each without its command.
research: GPT answers, Claude checks every source
in one check of research tools, written with Claude's help, none of the 82 checked sources from Opus 5.5 failed. https://magpieindex.com/guides/best-ai-deep-research-tools
ask viktor your question with `!gpt` and ask for linked sources. in my test, a market question on GPT came back with two linked surveys.
then send this in the same chat:
 
every claim returns with a quote from its source, and a mark on each one the source does not back.
without viktor, ask ChatGPT the same question with linked sources. then paste the same check into a chat on Opus 5.5, without the command at the start and with ChatGPT's answer in place of "the reply above".
 
nothing ships until a second model has quoted every line it doubts.
run the review on the next piece of code before it ships.
 
04. a top model only where a wrong answer costs you
the first urge is to put every job on a top model, to be safe. 02 showed it pays off only on the jobs marked yes.
with viktor: one default for the team
viktor's team mode sets the default model for the whole workspace. he has four: Ultra for the hardest work, Smart for everyday work and the default, Balanced for routine volume, Cheap for quick lookups.
his Settings page prices each mode against Smart: Ultra at about 1.3x the cost, Balanced about 45% cheaper, Cheap about 90% cheaper.
an admin sets the team mode as the Workspace default on the Model tab of his Settings. when you ask viktor to change a setting, he posts a card and waits for a click on Approve.
viktor runs on the mode and the models you set, and he does not pick them by himself.
with viktor: a model and a cap for each scheduled job
a scheduled job with no model of its own runs on the team mode.
viktor has no built-in spending limit for one job. ask for a monthly cap, and he adds a check that skips a run once the job has used its cap that month.
paste into viktor to set up both scheduled jobs:
 
in my test, viktor played the job back in under a minute with the job's model and a cap of 150 credits a month, about $0.38 on his own screen. he created nothing.
after my yes he did one test run that sent nothing, and the job showed up on his Tasks page with its own model.
say yes only when the playback names a model and a cap for each scheduled job.
 
 
before viktor, one plan paid the same for each job, small or costly.
without viktor: one plan
keep the family that wins most of the jobs on your card. its cheapest level costs $20 a month on Claude or ChatGPT.
inside it, a quick model works under the top one. a subagent is a helper the main agent hands a side job to.
Anthropic pairs Claude Haiku 5.5, its quick model, with Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 as a subagent on coding work. paste this into your coding agent:
 
pay for a higher plan only in the family that holds your costly list. live X is the one job only Grok does, and X Plus, $8 a month, includes it.
a top model now runs only on the jobs where a wrong answer costs you.
after a month, the spend shows which of these choices were worth it.
 
05. see where the money goes, and move fixed steps to a script
a job that runs every morning pays for thinking on every run, even when every run comes out the same. after a month, nobody remembers which job ate the money.
without viktor: the monthly cost sheet
on the 1st of the month, fill the cost sheet from 02 again, with a count of runs and two new columns:
 
slow down or pause the job nobody read.
with viktor: ask where the credits go
send this in your direct chat with him:
 
in my test, viktor answered in under a minute and changed nothing. he listed the five chats that cost the most, the model each ran on and its credits, with one fix for each.
i said yes to one fix only. viktor posted a card with Approve and Reject, and the change ran only after my click.
the fix moved the workspace default to Balanced, the team mode from 04 for routine volume.
i also asked how much the fix would save. viktor would not guess, and offered to compare the credits per plain message after a week.
so ask him again a week after any fix, and you see the real saving.
 
one message shows which job ate the month, and nothing changes until you say yes.
fixed steps go to a script
a script is a small program that repeats the same steps the same way every time, with no AI.
a developer on Zenn, a Japanese site for programmers, swapped an AI morning digest, a daily summary of new items, for a plain script. 

https://zenn.dev/taikikei/articles/951e0d3f735531?locale=en
of its 10 steps, only 1 needed a decision, and the running cost went to $0, down from $31 a month.
your own repeating job splits the same way. write it as steps and mark each one that comes out the same every run:
 
the yes steps can run as a script, and the no step keeps a model. paste the step list into the chat you already use, with this:
 
back comes a script for the yes steps and how to start it each morning, and nothing runs until your yes.
 
 
one paste that sets it all up
you now hold five habits that stay when the winners move:
who wins which job, on one card.
what each finished job costs.
a second family on every review.
the top model only on your costly list.
one monthly look at where the money goes.
the whole guide fits in one note of your own rules:
 
 
paste the note into a new chat in the app you use. it walks you through each line.
with one plan, put its models in rules 1 to 5 and run rule 2's review in a brand-new chat. live X needs Grok, and X Plus, $8 a month, includes it.
back come your seven rules, filled with your jobs.
tonight, send one job to the model that wins it and let a second family review it.
in viktor: a command per family, the team mode, a scheduled job with model and cap, and the credits check, each after your yes. hire him for your team.
